sentence: Gliclazide is a medicine for type 2 diabetes that belongs to a group called sulfonylureas.
note: NHS page title 'Gliclazide: medicine for type 2 diabetes'; Diabetes UK lists it as a sulphonylurea.

sentence: In type 2 diabetes the body does not make or use insulin well enough, so sugar builds up in the blood.
Diabetes UK says gliclazide comes as standard-release or slow-release tablets.
note: Second-pass search: Diabetes UK says standard-release or slow-release tablets.

sentence: Diabetes UK describes gliclazide as one of four sulphonylureas that people with type 2 diabetes in the UK can be prescribed.
note: Second-pass search: 'four types of sulphonylureas ... can be prescribed'.

sentence: The NHS says most adults and children aged 12 years and over can take it, but it is not suitable for everyone.
note: NHS 'Who can and cannot take gliclazide'.

sentence: The NHS lists type 1 diabetes, a past allergic reaction, diabetic ketoacidosis, severe kidney or liver disease, porphyria and G6PD deficiency among the reasons it may not be suitable.
note: NHS 'Who can and cannot take' summary, second-pass search.

sentence: Gliclazide works by prompting the pancreas to make more insulin.
note: NHS and Diabetes UK: prompts the pancreas to release more insulin.

sentence: Insulin is a hormone made in the pancreas that helps move sugar from the blood into the body's cells.
A UK formulary guide says gliclazide directly stimulates insulin release, so it has the potential to cause hypoglycaemia.
note: Buckinghamshire guide: 'directly stimulating insulin secretion, so has the potential for causing hypoglycaemia' (re-retrieved).

sentence: Diabetes UK lists tummy ache, sickness and diarrhoea among the common effects of sulphonylureas.
note: Second-pass search of Diabetes UK sulphonylureas page.

sentence: The NHS says side effects can be less likely if the tablets are taken with a meal.
note: Second-pass search of NHS side effects page.

sentence: Diabetes UK says some people gain weight while taking a sulphonylurea.
note: Second-pass search of Diabetes UK page.

sentence: Diabetes UK says rarer effects of sulphonylureas include liver damage and low blood cell counts.
note: Second-pass search of Diabetes UK page.

sentence: The NHS lists three rarer, serious problems: an allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), a problem with the blood cells and problems with the liver.
note: NHS side effects page, second-pass search.

sentence: Warning signs of a blood cell problem include paleness, unusual bleeding or bruising, a sore throat and fever, and a liver problem can turn the skin or the whites of the eyes yellow.
note: NHS side effects page, second-pass search.

sentence: The NHS says to call 999 for a suspected anaphylaxis, with signs such as a swollen throat or tongue, a raised itchy rash or difficulty breathing.
note: NHS side effects page, second-pass search.

sentence: For other suspected serious side effects the NHS says to call NHS 111.
note: Main NHS gliclazide page 111/999 structure; an older NHS side-effects page says a doctor or 111 for blood or liver signs.

sentence: Low blood sugar, called hypoglycaemia or a hypo, is a common side effect of gliclazide.
note: NHS: gliclazide can cause low blood sugar; Diabetes UK: one of the most common sulphonylurea side effects.

sentence: The NHS says it can cause dizziness, feeling sick, being very hungry or being very tired.
Diabetes UK says hypos are more likely when a meal is missed, after strenuous exercise or after drinking alcohol.
note: Second-pass search of Diabetes UK page.

sentence: The usual response the NHS describes is to eat or drink something sugary to raise blood sugar quickly.
The NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 if the sugary food or drink does not help or the symptoms return.
note: Second-pass search: 'Call your doctor or 111 if sugar doesn't help or hypo symptoms return' (NHS main page; search summary did not name the page precisely).

sentence: If a person with a hypo becomes unconscious, does not begin to regain consciousness, or shows signs of a seizure, NHS diabetes guidance says to call 999 straight away.
note: NHS Scotland My Diabetes My Way: unconscious or seizure, call 999 straight away; no regained consciousness after 10 minutes, call 999. The nhs.uk hypoglycaemia page itself was not retrieved with this wording.

sentence: NHS hospital guidance says nothing is given by mouth to someone who is unconscious or fitting, because of the risk of choking.
note: Royal Devon guide and several NHS trust leaflets: nothing by mouth, choking risk.

sentence: The NHS says a person who has taken more than the prescribed amount of gliclazide should call NHS 111.
note: Second-pass search of NHS gliclazide page.

sentence: The NHS says that if gliclazide makes a person feel sleepy or dizzy, they should not drive until the symptoms pass.
note: Second-pass search summary; page not named, medium confidence.

sentence: Diabetes UK says sulphonylureas can increase the risk of hypos while driving.
note: Second-pass search of Diabetes UK page.

sentence: DVLA guidance says a driver who has an episode of severe hypoglycaemia while driving must stop driving and tell the DVLA, and it defines severe as needing another person's help.
note: GOV.UK: Group 1 and 2 drivers with severe hypoglycaemia whilst driving must not drive and must notify DVLA.

sentence: The NHS says alcohol can be drunk with gliclazide but more alcohol can raise the risk of low blood sugar, while UK manufacturer leaflets say drinking alcohol is not recommended because it can alter diabetes control.
note: Second-pass search: NHS allows drinking with a limit warning; manufacturer leaflets stricter. The first pass said two NHS pages differ, which the re-check did not support.

sentence: The NHS says gliclazide is not usually used in pregnancy, and a doctor may offer a different medicine.
The NHS also advises against it during breastfeeding.
note: Second-pass search: NHS advises against while breastfeeding.

sentence: The NHS says some antibiotics and antifungals, steroid tablets, NSAID painkillers and other diabetes medicines can cause low blood sugar when taken with gliclazide.
The NHS says ibuprofen and aspirin should be checked with a pharmacist or doctor first, because they can lower blood sugar too much.
The NHS says St John's wort should not be taken, because it may change how the body processes gliclazide.
The NHS advises checking with a pharmacist or doctor before combining gliclazide with any medicine, herbal remedy, vitamin or supplement.
UK prescribing information lists miconazole, an antifungal, as a contraindicated combination because it increases the blood-sugar-lowering effect.
note: Several gliclazide SmPCs: miconazole contraindicated, increases hypoglycaemic effect.

sentence: The NHS says to tell the doctor before an operation, because gliclazide increases the risk of low blood sugar during surgery.
A UK formulary guide says HbA1c shows overall diabetes control but cannot show day-to-day swings in blood glucose or hypoglycaemia.
NICE advises considering short-term self-monitoring of blood glucose in adults with type 2 diabetes when starting corticosteroids or to confirm suspected hypoglycaemia.
NICE sets a different HbA1c aim for adults taking a drug associated with hypoglycaemia.
note: NG28 recommendations, second-pass search (53 vs 48 mmol/mol; figures not used).

sentence: The NHS says alcohol can be drunk with gliclazide, but more alcohol can raise the risk of low blood sugar.
UK manufacturer leaflets say drinking alcohol is not recommended because it can alter diabetes control.
Low blood sugar is called a hypo, and the NHS says the usual response is to eat or drink something sugary.
The NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 if sugary food or drink does not help or the symptoms return.
If the person becomes unconscious, does not begin to regain consciousness, or has signs of a seizure, NHS diabetes guidance says to call 999 straight away.
The NHS says gliclazide is not usually used in pregnancy, and a doctor may offer a different medicine.
The NHS also advises against it during breastfeeding.
The NHS says that if gliclazide makes a person feel sleepy or dizzy, they should not drive until the symptoms pass.
